```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 6,
                      fig.height = 4)
```

```{r setup}
library(lagprotest)
```

## The question

PROTEST [@jackson1995protest; @perezneto2001protest] measures how well two
multivariate configurations of the same observations match after Procrustes
superimposition, and tests that match by permutation. When the observations
are ordered time points, for example monthly means of a set of environmental
variables and of a set of phenotypic traits, concordance may be strongest not
between contemporaneous rows but after a delay: the response may track its
driver with a lag of *k* time units.

`lagged_protest()` asks at which lag the two series match best. For each
candidate lag *k*, row *t* of `X` is paired with row *t + k* of `Y`, the
series are truncated to their `n - k` overlapping rows, and the symmetric
Procrustes statistic *m*² is computed. Lower *m*² means stronger
concordance. Each lag is tested by permutation, and the lag with the
strongest evidence of concordance (by default, the smallest per-lag p-value)
is reported together with the full lag profile.

## Input data

Both inputs have one row per time point, in temporal order, and the same
number of rows. Columns are variables and need not be the same in number or
kind. `X` is the configuration expected to lead (the driver); `Y` the one
expected to follow. Inputs can be matrices, data frames or `dist` objects;
dissimilarities are converted to principal coordinates, so any dissimilarity
measure suited to the data can be used upstream.

Here we simulate a 12-month series of five variables (`X`) and a response
(`Y`) that follows `X` with a lag of two months:

```{r simulate}
sim <- simulate_lagged_series(n_times = 12, true_lag = 2, autocorr = 0.5,
                              noise_sd = 0.5, seed = 1)
dim(sim$X)
dim(sim$Y)
```

`simulate_lagged_series()` builds seasonal sinusoids plus AR(1) noise
(other seasonal shapes are available through `waveform`). With
`true_lag = NULL` it returns two independent series, which is useful for
checking Type I error.

## Running the test

```{r fit}
fit <- lagged_protest(sim$X, sim$Y, lags = 0:4, nperm = 999, seed = 1)
fit
```

By default the null distribution comes from phase-randomized surrogates of
`Y` (see [Choosing the permutation scheme](#choosing-the-permutation-scheme));
`seed` makes the result reproducible. The profile lists, for every lag, the
number of rows used (`n`), *m*², the Procrustes correlation
*r* = √(1 − *m*²), the permutation p-value and the number of surrogates. The
optimal lag here is the true one, 2.

The per-lag p-values are not corrected for testing several lags, nor for
choosing the optimal lag after looking at the profile.
Reporting the raw p-value at the optimal lag therefore inflates Type I error
to roughly the rate at which *any* lag is significant. The p-value to report
for the optimal lag is the global p-value, printed below the optimal lag and
stored in `fit$p.global`. It compares the smallest per-lag p-value with the
smallest per-lag p-value obtained under each permutation (the minP test of
Westfall and Young), so it is the p-value of the whole scan-and-select
procedure:

```{r global}
fit$p.global
```

Comparing lags by their p-values, rather than by *m*² itself, matters
because *m*² at lag *k* rests on `n − k` rows and is smaller and more
variable when fewer rows overlap. The smallest *m*² therefore tends to fall
at the longest lags even for independent series, and a test built on it has
less power for short lags. The argument `stat` chooses the statistic:
`"minP"` (default), `"z"` (*m*² standardized by its own null distribution)
or `"raw"` (the smallest *m*², used up to version 0.6). All three are valid
global tests computed from the same permutations:

```{r stat}
sapply(c("minP", "z", "raw"), function(s)
  lagged_protest(sim$X, sim$Y, lags = 0:4, seed = 1, stat = s)$p.global)
```

Per-lag p-values can also be corrected. `p.adjust.method = "maxT"` gives the
single-step adjusted p-value of every lag for the chosen `stat`, whose value at the
optimal lag equals the global p-value; any method of `stats::p.adjust()` can
be used instead, and raw and adjusted values are then both reported:

```{r holm}
fit_holm <- lagged_protest(sim$X, sim$Y, lags = 0:4, permutation = "cyclic",
                           stat = "z", p.adjust.method = "holm")
fit_holm$profile[, c("lag", "p.value", "p.adjusted")]
```

With the cyclic scheme and `n = 12` there are only 22 permutations, so a
raw p-value at its minimum of 0.043 becomes 0.217 after Holm correction
across five lags, and significance at α = 0.05 is unattainable
(see Caveats).

`summary()` returns the profile as a data frame, with the optimal lag
flagged, and prints the global p-value and the effect measures described
next below it:

```{r summary}
summary(fit)
```

## Strength of the association

A p-value is bounded by the number of permutations and mixes the strength
of an association with the length of the series. `lagged_protest()`
therefore also returns continuous measures, computed from the same
permutations:

```{r effect}
fit$effect
```

At each lag, `z` in the profile is the observed *m*² standardized by the
mean and standard deviation of its permutation null, with the sign reversed
so that larger values mean stronger concordance, and `a` is the concordance
relative to the null mean. The effect lag is the lag of the largest `z`.
`Z` is the position of that largest `z` among the largest `z` of each
permutation, in standard deviations; `A` and the corrected RV coefficient
are scaled so that 0 is the value expected by chance and 1 is perfect
concordance. All three are near 0 for independent series.

The effect lag and the optimal lag usually agree, because both place every
lag on the scale of its own null distribution; with `stat = "z"` they are
the same by definition. With `stat = "raw"` they differ more often, because
the smallest *m*² tends to fall at the longest lags. `print()` notes when
the two differ (see Caveats).

`fit$ar1` gives the mean lag-1 autocorrelation of the columns of each
series, raw and after removing the seasonal harmonics. It is descriptive,
and helps judge whether the series are short and strongly autocorrelated
enough for the phase scheme to be liberal (see Caveats):

```{r ar1}
fit$ar1
```

## Plotting the lag profile

```{r plot, fig.alt = "Lag profile: m2 against lag, with a dashed line for the 5% quantile of the permutation null distribution at each lag."}
plot(fit)
```

The solid line is the observed *m*² at each lag. The dashed line is the 5%
quantile of the permutation null distribution at that lag: observed values
below it are significant at α = 0.05 before correction. Filled points mark
lags with p < 0.05 (after adjustment, if one was requested), the dotted
vertical line marks the optimal lag, and the circle around it is filled
when the global p-value is below 0.05. `ggplot2::autoplot(fit)` draws the
same plot with ggplot2, and `as.data.frame(fit)` returns the data behind it.

## Residuals per observation

Procrustes residuals show which time points fit the superimposition well
and which deviate, at the optimal lag:

```{r residuals}
residuals(fit)
```

Each row pairs a time point of `X` (`x_row`) with the time point of `Y` it is
matched to (`y_row`). Row names of the inputs, such as month labels, are
carried through.

## Choosing the permutation scheme

Standard PROTEST permutes rows freely, which assumes that time points are
exchangeable under the null hypothesis. Seasonal or otherwise autocorrelated
series are not: two independent series that both cycle annually will often
look concordant against a null that destroys their temporal structure, a
problem shared with other permutation tests on autocorrelated data
[@legendre2002spatial].

`lagged_protest()` offers two schemes that keep the temporal structure of
`Y`:

* `permutation = "phase"` (default) draws `nperm` phase-randomized
  surrogates of `Y` [@ebisuzaki1997]. Each surrogate keeps the amplitude
  spectrum of every column of `Y`, and hence its autocorrelation, as well as
  the cross-spectra among the columns, but receives new Fourier phases.
* `permutation = "cyclic"` shifts the full `Y` series cyclically by
  1, …, n − 1 positions, and also time-reverses it when `mirror = TRUE`,
  *before* the lag is applied. Each permuted series keeps its
  autocorrelation. All shifts are enumerated, so the test needs no random
  seed.

`permutation = "free"` reproduces the behavior of `vegan::protest()`
[@vegan].

The cyclic and phase schemes differ in how they handle the scan across lags.
Shifting `Y` by *s* positions and then applying lag *k* pairs the same rows
as lag *k* + *s* without a shift. When several lags are scanned, some cyclic
permutations therefore reproduce the observed alignment at another lag, and
the null distribution of the minimum *m*² across lags contains the signal
itself. The per-lag p-values are unaffected, but the global p-value loses
power. Phase surrogates are new series rather than shifts of the observed
one, so they avoid this problem; they also allow as many surrogates as
desired, instead of the `2(n − 1)` cyclic permutations.

The choice matters. Under independence, a small simulation with 24 monthly
samples spanning one cycle gives the following rejection rates at α = 0.05:
for the raw p-value at the optimal lag, and for the global p-value under each
scheme. A second set of series, in which `Y` follows `X` with a lag of two,
gives the power of the global p-value. The simulation uses `stat = "raw"`
because with only 99 surrogates and five lags `"minP"` cannot reach
p < 0.05 (it needs at least 100 permutations per lag):

```{r calibration}
rates <- function(true_lag, n_rep) {
  res <- vapply(seq_len(n_rep), function(i) {
    s <- simulate_lagged_series(n_times = 24, period = 24, true_lag = true_lag,
                                autocorr = 0.5, noise_sd = 0.5, seed = i)
    cyc <- lagged_protest(s$X, s$Y, lags = 0:4, permutation = "cyclic",
                          stat = "raw")
    pha <- lagged_protest(s$X, s$Y, lags = 0:4, permutation = "phase",
                          nperm = 99, seed = i, stat = "raw")
    fre <- lagged_protest(s$X, s$Y, lags = 0:4, permutation = "free",
                          nperm = 99, seed = i, stat = "raw")
    c(cyclic_optimal_raw = cyc$p.value, cyclic_global = cyc$p.global,
      phase_global = pha$p.global, free_global = fre$p.global)
  }, numeric(4))
  rowMeans(res < 0.05)
}
rbind(type_I = rates(NULL, 100), power = rates(2, 100))
```

The raw p-value at the optimal lag is too liberal and free permutation
rejects almost always. Both global p-values keep Type I error near the
nominal level, but only the phase scheme retains power.

## Caveats

* **Complete cycles and shared periodicity.** Both the cyclic and the phase
  schemes treat the series as periodic with period `n`. This is appropriate
  when the series spans whole cycles, such as 12 monthly samples of an
  annual cycle. Cyclic-shift null models can be biased when this does not
  hold [@kalyuzhny2020cyclic]. In simulations with this package, two
  independent seasonal series whose period differed from the series length
  were declared concordant far more often than α under either scheme:
  series with the same period trace the same trajectory shape, which
  Procrustes rotation can superimpose whatever the phase difference.
  Supplying the length of the cycle with `period` truncates both series to
  whole cycles (e.g., the first 18 of 24 monthly samples for an 18-month
  cycle), which brought the Type I error back to the level of series that
  span complete cycles, at the cost of the rows dropped.
  Removing the seasonal component by harmonic regression did not: it
  reduced the excess but left the test liberal, and it removes the seasonal
  signal that is often the object of the analysis.
* **Strong autocorrelation.** In simulations with 1000 replicates per
  scenario, the global p-value of the phase scheme kept Type I error at
  0.047–0.053 for AR(1) autocorrelation up to 0.5, but reached 0.063 at 0.7
  and 0.129 at 0.9 (averaged over series length and number of variables),
  and 0.15–0.19 with 12–24 time points or 10 variables. The excess faded
  with longer series (0.063 at AR(1) = 0.9 with 96 time points). The cyclic
  scheme without mirror was less affected (0.081 at 0.9) but had much lower
  power. For short, strongly autocorrelated series, report the cyclic
  result alongside the phase one, and estimate the autocorrelation of the
  series.
* **Few permutations.** With `n` time points there are only `2(n − 1)`
  cyclic permutations, so the smallest attainable p-value is
  `1 / (2(n − 1) + 1)`, 0.043 for `n = 12`. Corrections across many lags may
  then be unattainable at α = 0.05. The phase scheme has no such floor.
* **Different window sizes.** *m*² at lag *k* is based on `n − k` rows, so
  long lags rest on fewer observations, and the smallest *m*² tends to fall
  at the longest lags scanned even for independent series. The default
  `stat = "minP"` removes this bias from the global test and the optimal
  lag; with `stat = "raw"`, an optimal lag at the end of the scan should be
  compared with the effect lag in `fit$effect`. In all cases, keep candidate
  lags within a range justified by the biology of the system.
* **Scaling.** With `scale = TRUE` (default) variables are standardized on
  the full series before truncation.

## Several data sets

`lagged_protest_pairs()` runs `lagged_protest()` on every pair of data sets
in a named list (or on chosen pairs), scanning both directions through the
sign of the lag, and adjusts the global p-values across pairs. The article
[Seasonal liver plasticity in a treefrog](https://provetelab.org/lagprotest/articles/liver-example.html)
applies it to the `dminutus_liver` data set.
